resources.label: Microsoft Learn: Describe Azure architecture and services
Microsoft Learn: Describe Azure management and governance

flashcards.back: The delivery of computing services — servers, storage, databases, networking, software — over the internet, with pay-as-you-go pricing instead of buying and maintaining physical infrastructure.
flashcards.detail: This is the baseline definition the whole exam builds on. If a question describes 'renting' IT resources instead of owning them, it's pointing at this.

flashcards.back: A framework describing which security and management tasks the cloud provider handles versus the customer. The split shifts depending on IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS — the customer always keeps responsibility for their data and identities.
flashcards.detail: Exam trap: no matter how much Microsoft manages, the customer is never off the hook for securing their own data and accounts.

flashcards.front: Public vs. private vs. hybrid cloud
flashcards.back: Public: resources owned and shared by a third-party provider. Private: dedicated to one organization, on-premises or hosted. Hybrid: combines both, often for compliance or a gradual migration.
flashcards.detail: A healthcare org keeping patient records on-prem while running its website in Azure is a classic hybrid scenario.

flashcards.back: Pricing where you pay only for the resources you actually use, instead of a large upfront purchase.
flashcards.detail: This is the mechanism behind the CapEx-to-OpEx shift the exam likes to test.

flashcards.back: CapEx is large upfront capital spending on infrastructure you own. OpEx is ongoing operating expense — paying for what you use as you use it. Cloud computing shifts spending from CapEx toward OpEx.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario mentions avoiding a big hardware purchase, that's the CapEx-to-OpEx shift, not just 'saving money' in the abstract.

flashcards.back: A model where the provider manages the infrastructure automatically, and you're billed based on execution rather than provisioned capacity — you write code without managing servers.
flashcards.detail: Azure Functions is the canonical serverless example on this exam.

flashcards.back: Scalability is the general ability to handle more load by adding resources, manually or automatically. Elasticity specifically means resources scale up and down automatically in response to real-time demand.
flashcards.detail: Elasticity is a specific kind of scalability — the automatic, dynamic kind. Not every scalable system is elastic.

flashcards.back: Reliability means a system recovers from failures and keeps functioning. Predictability means consistent performance and cost, so you can plan capacity and budget confidently.
flashcards.detail: An unpredictable, spiky bill is a sign predictability isn't being managed well, even if the system is technically reliable.

flashcards.back: IaaS: rent infrastructure (VMs, storage, networking), you manage the OS and up. PaaS: rent a platform, you manage just your app and data. SaaS: rent a finished application, you just use it.
flashcards.detail: Microsoft 365 is the textbook SaaS example. Azure App Service is the textbook PaaS example.

flashcards.back: Moving from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS gives you more that's managed for you, but less direct control. Match the scenario's control needs to the right type.
flashcards.detail: If a question stresses 'wants full control of the OS,' that's IaaS. If it stresses 'just wants the app to work,' that's SaaS.

flashcards.back: A discounted pricing option for unused Azure capacity, in exchange for accepting that the VM can be evicted with little notice if Azure needs that capacity back.
flashcards.detail: The trade-off — big discount for interruption risk — makes Spot the right answer for low-priority, interruption-tolerant workloads, never for anything mission-critical.

flashcards.back: A region is a set of datacenters in a geographic area. Region pairs are two regions in the same geography, at least 300 miles apart, used for disaster recovery — updates roll out to only one region in a pair at a time.
flashcards.detail: The 300-mile / same-geography detail is a specific fact the exam likes to test directly.

flashcards.back: Physically and logically isolated Azure regions for specific compliance needs, like Azure Government, operated separately from global Azure.
flashcards.detail: These exist specifically so certain government or regulatory data never touches the general commercial cloud.

flashcards.back: Physically separate datacenters within an Azure region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking, used to protect against a single datacenter failing.
flashcards.detail: Region = geography. Availability zone = specific datacenter within that geography. An availability zone does NOT protect against a whole region going down.

flashcards.back: A resource is any deployable item in Azure, like a VM or database. A resource group is a logical container holding related resources that you deploy, manage, and delete as a group — and can contain resources from more than one region.
flashcards.detail: Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it — a common 'what happens if' exam scenario.

flashcards.back: A logical container that groups resource groups together, tied to billing and access management. An organization can have multiple subscriptions for different departments or environments.
flashcards.detail: Subscriptions sit above resource groups and below management groups in the hierarchy.

flashcards.back: Containers that group multiple subscriptions together, letting you apply governance policies, like Azure Policy or RBAC, across many subscriptions at once.
flashcards.detail: Useful for a large org that wants one security policy applied to every subscription without configuring each one separately. Deleting a management group does not delete the subscriptions inside it.

flashcards.back: From broadest to narrowest: management groups, then subscriptions, then resource groups, then individual resources. Settings applied higher up flow down and compound going down.
flashcards.detail: A policy added at a lower scope can make things more restrictive than the parent required, but never less.

flashcards.back: VMs: full control, you manage the OS. Containers: lightweight, package an app with its dependencies, more portable than a VM. Functions: run small pieces of code on demand, fully serverless.
flashcards.detail: As you move VM → container → function, management overhead drops and portability/scalability generally goes up.

flashcards.back: Scale Sets automatically add or remove identical VMs based on demand or schedule. Availability sets group VMs so they don't all update or fail at once, within one datacenter. Azure Virtual Desktop delivers virtual desktops or apps to users.
flashcards.detail: Scale Sets are about scaling out. Availability sets are about not losing everything at once during maintenance or a single-datacenter failure — not a whole-region failure.

flashcards.back: Web apps (App Service, PaaS, easiest), containers (more portable, more control), and virtual machines (most control, most management overhead) — pick based on how much you want to manage.
flashcards.detail: App Service is the go-to answer when a scenario just needs 'a website, minimal management.'

flashcards.back: A virtual network (VNet) is a private network in Azure. Subnets divide it into smaller segments. Peering connects VNets. Azure DNS resolves names. VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute connect on-premises networks to Azure.
flashcards.detail: VPN Gateway travels over the public internet, encrypted. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated connection — and is NOT encrypted by default, since it relies on the private connection itself.

flashcards.back: A public endpoint is reachable over the internet. A private endpoint gives a resource a private IP inside your VNet, so traffic never leaves the Microsoft network.
flashcards.detail: Private endpoints are the answer whenever a scenario wants to reduce internet exposure for a resource like a database.

flashcards.back: Blob (unstructured data), Files (managed file shares), Queue (messaging), and Table (NoSQL key-value) storage are the core Azure Storage services, all held within a storage account.
flashcards.detail: The storage account is the top-level container; blobs, files, queues, and tables live inside it.

flashcards.back: Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive tiers balance storage cost against access speed and retrieval cost — Hot is most expensive to store but cheapest/fastest to access, Archive is the opposite.
flashcards.detail: Archive tier data can take hours to retrieve — a scenario needing frequent, fast access should never point to Archive, but one needing cheap, rarely-touched long-term storage does.

flashcards.back: LRS keeps copies in one datacenter. ZRS spreads copies across availability zones in one region. GRS/GZRS copies to a secondary paired region for disaster recovery. RA-GRS (or RA-GZRS) adds read access to that secondary region even before a failover happens.
flashcards.detail: Plain GRS isn't readable from the secondary region until failover — the read-access ('RA-') variants are the ones you can read from directly, at any time.

flashcards.front: AzCopy vs. Storage Explorer vs. Azure File Sync
flashcards.back: AzCopy is a command-line tool for scripted, one-time or bulk file transfers into Azure Storage. Storage Explorer is a GUI tool for browsing and managing storage data. Azure File Sync keeps an on-premises file server continuously synchronized with an Azure file share.
flashcards.detail: File Sync is the odd one out — it's ongoing synchronization, not a one-time transfer tool like the other two.

flashcards.front: Azure Migrate vs. Azure Data Box
flashcards.back: Azure Migrate assesses and migrates on-premises servers and workloads into Azure, typically over the network. Azure Data Box is a physical device shipped to you for transferring very large datasets when network transfer would be too slow.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario mentions terabytes of data and a slow internet connection, that's pointing at Data Box, not Migrate.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management service, formerly Azure Active Directory. Manages users, groups, and access to apps and resources.
flashcards.detail: Renamed from Azure AD — expect both names to appear in materials, but Entra ID is the current name.

flashcards.back: Single sign-on: one login for multiple apps. Multifactor authentication: a second verification step beyond a password. Passwordless: authentication without a password at all, like a security key or authenticator app.
flashcards.detail: These three get tested as distinct concepts — don't conflate MFA with passwordless, they're different approaches.

flashcards.back: Lets people outside your organization, like partners or customers, sign in using their own identities rather than you creating them a new account in your directory.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer when a scenario mentions collaborating with an outside company without issuing them internal accounts. Microsoft Entra External ID is the current product family for this.

flashcards.back: Policies that grant or block access based on conditions like user location, device compliance state, or risk level — for example, requiring MFA only when signing in from an unfamiliar location.
flashcards.detail: Conditional Access is about the conditions under which access is allowed — not just location, but device state, app, and risk level too — distinct from RBAC which is about what access is granted.

flashcards.back: Role-based access control assigns permissions to users, groups, or applications at a specific scope — management group, subscription, resource group, or resource — following least-privilege principles.
flashcards.detail: RBAC answers 'what can this identity do,' Conditional Access answers 'under what conditions can they do it.'

flashcards.back: A security model that assumes no user or device is trusted by default, even inside the network perimeter — every request is verified based on identity, device, and context.
flashcards.detail: "Never trust, always verify" is the one-line summary. This is the answer when a scenario shows a perimeter breach that still fails to grant access.

flashcards.back: A layered security strategy — physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, and data layers — so that if one layer is breached, others still protect the resource.
flashcards.detail: Think of it as concentric rings of security around your data, not a single wall — related to, but distinct from, Zero Trust.

flashcards.back: A tool that assesses your security posture across Azure, hybrid, and other-cloud resources and gives recommendations to improve it, plus threat protection for workloads.
flashcards.detail: Defender for Cloud is narrower and security-specific. Azure Advisor is broader, covering cost, reliability, and performance too.

flashcards.back: An automatically-managed Entra ID identity for an Azure resource, like a VM or Function, letting it authenticate to other Azure services without embedding credentials in code.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer whenever a scenario wants passwordless, credential-free authentication between Azure services.

flashcards.back: Resource type, usage/consumption, region, and licensing all affect what you pay in Azure.
flashcards.detail: Region matters because pricing varies by datacenter location — a detail that's easy to overlook.

flashcards.back: The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of Azure resources you plan to use. The Total Cost of Ownership calculator compares your current on-premises infrastructure cost against running it in Azure over time.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario asks 'should we move to the cloud at all,' that's the TCO calculator. If it asks 'what will this specific setup cost,' that's the Pricing calculator.

flashcards.back: Name/value pairs attached to resources for organizing and tracking, like by department or environment — useful for cost reporting and filtering in Cost Management.
flashcards.detail: Tags don't affect how a resource functions, only how it's organized and reported on.

flashcards.back: A unified data governance service that helps you discover, classify, and protect sensitive data across your organization, including hybrid, non-Azure sources.
flashcards.detail: Purview is about knowing what data you have and how sensitive it is, not about access control itself.

flashcards.back: Enforces organizational rules on resources, for example requiring a specific region or blocking a VM size, and evaluates and reports on compliance — it can even deny non-compliant deployments outright.
flashcards.detail: Policy governs how resources must be configured. RBAC governs who can act on them — a distinction the exam tests directly.

flashcards.back: A Delete lock blocks deletion only. A Read-only lock blocks both deletion and modification. Both override a user's normal permissions, regardless of what RBAC otherwise allows.
flashcards.detail: Exam trap: a Delete lock will NOT stop someone from modifying a resource's settings — only a Read-only lock does that.

flashcards.back: The Azure portal is the web GUI. Cloud Shell is a browser-based command line, no local install needed. Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell are command-line tools installed locally for scripting — four ways to manage the same resources.
flashcards.detail: Cloud Shell running in the browser is what distinguishes it from CLI/PowerShell installed on your own machine.

flashcards.back: IaC means defining infrastructure in code or config files instead of manual clicks, so deployments are repeatable and version-controllable. ARM templates are Azure's native JSON format for declaring what resources to deploy.
flashcards.detail: Repeatability and version control are the key benefits IaC brings that clicking through the portal doesn't.

flashcards.back: A free tool that analyzes your resource configuration and usage, then gives personalized recommendations across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance.
flashcards.detail: Advisor is broad (cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, performance). Defender for Cloud is specifically security-focused.

flashcards.back: Collects and analyzes telemetry from your Azure resources — Log Analytics stores and queries logs, Azure Monitor alerts notify you of conditions, and Application Insights monitors live applications.
flashcards.detail: Log Analytics is the query/storage layer inside Azure Monitor, not a separate standalone product.

flashcards.back: Extends Azure management tools, like Azure Policy and RBAC, to resources outside Azure — on-premises servers, other clouds, or edge devices — managed with the same tools as native Azure resources.
flashcards.detail: Arc is the answer whenever a scenario wants 'one pane of glass' for Azure plus non-Azure infrastructure.

flashcards.back: Reports on the health of the Azure platform itself — like an ongoing outage in a region — separate from the health of your own specific resources.
flashcards.detail: Service Health = is Azure itself having a problem. Azure Monitor = is my stuff having a problem. Different questions, different tools.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's formal, measurable commitment to an uptime or performance target for a service, such as 99.9% monthly uptime, backed by service credits if the target is missed.
flashcards.detail: An SLA is a commitment with a financial remedy, not a guarantee of zero downtime — a distinction the exam tests directly.

flashcards.back: The effective SLA of a solution built from multiple dependent services. Chaining services in sequence multiplies their individual uptime percentages, producing a LOWER composite SLA than any single component. Adding redundant, independent components in parallel can raise the composite SLA above any one component's own figure.
flashcards.detail: Exam trap: depending on more services in sequence generally lowers your overall SLA, even though each individual piece still meets its own target.

flashcards.back: Basic support is free and included with every subscription, covering billing and subscription questions. Paid tiers — Developer, Standard, and Professional Direct — add technical support with progressively faster guaranteed response times for production issues. Microsoft Unified support (the current name for what was once called Premier) sits above these as a broader, account-managed enterprise offering rather than just another response-time tier.
flashcards.detail: Basic support alone has no response-time commitment for a production-down technical issue — that requires a paid tier.

flashcards.back: A licensing benefit that lets you apply existing on-premises Windows Server or SQL Server licenses (with active Software Assurance or an eligible subscription) toward the cost of running those workloads in Azure, instead of paying for a new license.
flashcards.detail: A separate cost lever from Reservations or Spot pricing — it reduces the licensing portion of the bill, not the underlying compute rate.

flashcards.back: A set of allow/deny security rules that filter inbound and outbound network traffic to Azure resources, based on source/destination IP, port, and protocol — applied at a subnet or an individual network interface.
flashcards.detail: NSGs are the baseline traffic-filtering tool on this exam; Azure Firewall is a more advanced managed alternative, but NSGs are the AZ-900-level answer.

flashcards.back: Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), distributing traffic by IP and port with no awareness of content. Application Gateway works at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), routing by URL path or host header, and can add a Web Application Firewall.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario mentions routing by URL path or needing a WAF, that's Application Gateway, not Load Balancer.

flashcards.back: A managed Kubernetes service for orchestrating, scaling, and self-healing groups of containers across a cluster of nodes — Azure manages the control plane, you manage your workloads.
flashcards.detail: AKS is the answer for orchestrating many containers at scale; Azure Container Instances is the answer for running one or a few standalone containers quickly, with no orchestration layer.

flashcards.back: A concise, domain-specific language for defining Azure infrastructure as code, which compiles down to standard ARM template JSON and deploys through the same Azure Resource Manager.
flashcards.detail: Bicep is Microsoft's current recommended way to author IaC on Azure — easier to read and write than raw ARM JSON, but functionally equivalent underneath.

flashcards.back: A deployment strategy that deliberately uses more than one public cloud provider, for example Azure alongside another provider, to avoid depending on a single vendor or to use each provider's strongest services.
flashcards.detail: Distinct from hybrid cloud: hybrid mixes on-premises/private infrastructure with public cloud; multi-cloud mixes two or more public cloud providers.

flashcards.front: Azure CDN vs. Azure Front Door
flashcards.back: Azure CDN caches static content at edge points-of-presence close to users to cut latency. Azure Front Door adds global HTTP(S) load balancing, path-based routing, and an optional Web Application Firewall on top of an edge network, for full web-application delivery, not just static caching.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario needs only 'serve images/video faster worldwide,' that's CDN. If it also needs routing logic or a WAF at the edge, that's Front Door, which is also where Microsoft is steering new work: Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) is slated for retirement in 2027.

flashcards.back: The set of tools for analyzing spend (Cost Analysis), setting spending alerts (budgets), and viewing and paying invoices, across one or more subscriptions.
flashcards.detail: This is where the factors that drive Azure costs show up as real, analyzable numbers, and where the estimates from the Pricing and TCO calculators get checked against what you actually spend.

flashcards.back: A pre-configured environment — subscriptions, management groups, policy, and a network baseline already in place — that a new workload lands into, instead of starting from a blank subscription every time.
flashcards.detail: A landing zone bakes governance into the resource hierarchy up front, so a new workload inherits compliant Azure Policy and Azure RBAC instead of every project reinventing it.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's guidance for evaluating a workload against five pillars — reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, and performance efficiency — used to weigh trade-offs against each other rather than optimizing just one in isolation.
flashcards.detail: Azure Advisor's recommendations are aligned with these same pillars and are generated automatically from your actual resources, flagging where a workload falls short.

flashcards.back: Lets a service provider or central IT team manage resources across multiple Azure tenants from within their own tenant, without switching directories or needing a separate guest account in each customer's tenant.
flashcards.detail: This is specifically for cross-tenant management at scale — an MSP managing dozens of customer tenants is the classic scenario, distinct from Azure RBAC, which governs access within a single tenant.

flashcards.back: A service for securely storing and tightly controlling access to secrets, encryption keys, and certificates, so they never sit hardcoded in application source code. An app typically authenticates to it using a managed identity rather than an embedded credential, with access to individual secrets still governed through Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC like any other resource.
flashcards.detail: Key Vault is the answer whenever a scenario wants to eliminate a hardcoded connection string or API key from source code entirely.

flashcards.back: A managed service that provides secure RDP and SSH access to virtual machines directly through the Azure portal over TLS, without needing a public endpoint on the VM itself or a client-side VPN. It works alongside a network security group (NSG) rather than replacing it — the NSG still filters what traffic is allowed to reach the VM's subnet in the first place.
flashcards.detail: Bastion is the answer whenever a scenario wants to remove a VM's exposed public RDP/SSH port while still allowing administrators to connect.

flashcards.back: A managed service that takes scheduled, application-consistent backups of Azure VMs, SQL databases, and other workloads into a Recovery Services vault. Those recovery points are protected by the vault's own storage redundancy setting — LRS, ZRS, or GRS (the default) — so the backup data can survive a datacenter failure, or with GRS a regional one.
flashcards.detail: Azure Backup protects data that already exists by restoring it after loss or corruption; it's a different job from Site Recovery, which keeps a whole workload running by replicating it to fail over to.

questions.question: A startup wants to launch quickly with minimal infrastructure management, but portability to another cloud provider later matters more to them than convenience today. Which service model best serves that stated priority?
options: IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
A Reserved Instance commitment on a single VM family
questions.explanation: IaaS resources like VMs are the most portable between providers, since they're closer to raw infrastructure. PaaS launches faster but leans on provider-specific platform features that make leaving harder — a real trade-off, and the question asks which priority wins. A Reserved Instance is a pricing commitment, not a service model, and doesn't address portability at all.
questions.whyTested: AZ-900 likes stacking two competing priorities (speed today vs. portability later) in one scenario to see if you'll default to the 'easiest'-sounding answer instead of the one the question actually asked for — real projects make this exact trade-off, so exams probe whether you noticed which priority was stated as the deciding one.

questions.question: A finance team complains their monthly Azure bill is unpredictable and spikes randomly, even though nothing about their workload has changed. Which cloud characteristic is failing here?
options: High availability
Predictability
Scalability
Elasticity
questions.explanation: Predictability is about consistent, forecastable cost and performance — an erratic bill with unchanged usage signals this isn't being managed well. Scalability, availability, and elasticity all describe how resources respond to load, not billing consistency.

questions.question: An operations team manually adds two web servers the day before a product launch and removes them a week later. A colleague describes this as 'the app's elasticity at work.' Which term correctly describes what happened?
options: Scalability but not elasticity, because the change was planned and manual
Elasticity, because capacity both increased and later decreased again
Neither, because only automatic changes count as scaling at all
Elasticity for the scale-out step, and scalability for the later scale-in
questions.explanation: Scalability is the general ability to handle more load by adding resources, whether a human does it or not — which is exactly what this team did. Elasticity is the narrower, automatic form: capacity grows and shrinks in response to real-time demand without an administrator planning it. Growing and shrinking is not enough to make it elastic if each step was manual; manual changes still count as scaling; and the direction of the change (out versus in) has nothing to do with which term applies.

questions.question: A company currently spends heavily on capital equipment refreshes every three years for its datacenter. Moving fully to Azure IaaS would primarily shift this spending pattern to:
options: A one-time Reserved Instance prepayment classified as CapEx
OpEx
A smaller but still recurring CapEx
No change in spending pattern
questions.explanation: Cloud computing shifts organizations from large upfront capital purchases toward ongoing operating expense. Even an upfront Reserved Instance purchase is still billed as a discounted rate on consumption — it is still a consumption commitment billed through Azure, not an equipment purchase, so it is not CapEx — a commonly missed distinction.

questions.question: Which of these best illustrates the shared responsibility model shifting MORE responsibility to Microsoft, compared with a self-managed deployment?
options: Moving a file server to an Azure VM running the same OS as before
Assigning an additional RBAC role to the team managing a self-managed VM
Enabling a Read-only resource lock on a self-managed VM
Moving a database to Azure SQL Database (PaaS) instead of a self-managed SQL Server on a VM
questions.explanation: PaaS services like Azure SQL Database hand OS patching and infrastructure management to Microsoft, shifting more of the split toward the provider than a lift-and-shift VM does. A resource lock or an RBAC assignment changes who on your team can do what — it doesn't move any responsibility to Microsoft at all.

questions.question: A team wants to run a low-priority batch job at the lowest possible cost, and can tolerate the job being interrupted and restarted if Azure needs the capacity back. Which pricing approach fits?
options: Standard pay-as-you-go pricing
Reserved instances
Spot pricing
An Azure Savings Plan for compute
questions.explanation: Spot pricing offers deep discounts in exchange for the possibility of eviction with little notice — ideal for interruption-tolerant, low-priority work. Reserved instances and Savings Plans both trade a usage commitment for a discount, but neither involves eviction risk, so neither passes on the deepest possible discount this scenario allows for.

questions.question: A company uses Microsoft 365 for email, Azure App Service for its website, and SQL Server installed on an Azure virtual machine. A new hire claims the company 'uses no IaaS at all.' Which correction is accurate?
options: The SQL Server VM is IaaS; App Service is PaaS and Microsoft 365 is SaaS
App Service is IaaS, because the company deploys its own code to it
Microsoft 365 is IaaS, because it runs on infrastructure Microsoft owns
Both App Service and the VM are IaaS, since both host company workloads
questions.explanation: Installing SQL Server on a VM means the company manages the guest OS and everything above it — the defining trait of IaaS. App Service is PaaS: deploying your own code to a managed runtime is what PaaS is for, not a sign of IaaS. Microsoft 365 is a finished application the company only consumes (SaaS); the fact that it runs on Microsoft-owned hardware is true of every cloud model and doesn't make it IaaS. Hosting a workload isn't the test either — what matters is which layers the customer manages.

questions.question: A retailer's site traffic multiplies 10x during a single holiday weekend, then returns to normal a few days later. Which cloud characteristic most directly and cost-effectively addresses this, as opposed to simply over-provisioning fixed capacity year-round?
options: Zero Trust
Elasticity
Availability sets
Reserved Instances
questions.explanation: Elasticity lets resources scale up automatically for the surge and back down afterward, avoiding paying for peak capacity year-round. Availability sets protect against hardware failure, not demand spikes, and Reserved Instances lock in a fixed commitment — the opposite of what a short, unpredictable spike calls for.

questions.question: Why might an organization choose a hybrid cloud model even though it's more complex to manage than pure public cloud?
options: Hybrid deployments typically cost less overall than pure public cloud once egress and support fees are added in
Moving fully to public cloud removes the need to manage identity for any on-premises systems that remain
Regulatory or data residency requirements may require some data to stay on-premises
Azure's regional footprint covers most countries, which usually removes data residency as a reason to go hybrid
questions.explanation: Compliance and data residency needs are a common, legitimate reason to keep some workloads on-premises while using public cloud elsewhere — some regulations specifically require certain data to stay off public cloud infrastructure entirely, not just within a given country's borders. Hybrid isn't reliably cheaper once you factor in running two environments, and identity still has to be managed for whatever on-premises systems remain, typically unified with something like Microsoft Entra ID rather than eliminated.
questions.whyTested: This question isn't really testing whether you know what hybrid cloud is — it's testing whether you can spot a plausible-sounding but wrong justification for it, since three of the four options reference real IT concepts (cost, identity, regional coverage) just slightly misapplied. Exams pair a correct-but-unglamorous answer like compliance against tempting distractors to see if you're pattern-matching keywords instead of reasoning through the actual claim being made.

questions.question: A finance department wants to compare five years of projected on-premises costs against five years of projected Azure costs before deciding whether to migrate at all. Which tool fits?
options: Azure Advisor
The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator
The Azure Pricing calculator
Azure Cost Management
questions.explanation: The TCO calculator is built specifically to compare projected on-premises cost against projected Azure cost before a migration decision. The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of specific Azure resources you already plan to deploy, and Cost Management/Advisor both analyze spend on resources you already have running — none of the other three compare against an on-premises baseline.

questions.question: A CIO's migration business case lists four expected benefits of moving to Azure. Which one should be removed because it misstates how Azure works?
options: Capacity can be added in minutes without a hardware procurement cycle
Spreading a workload across availability zones can raise its availability
Microsoft takes over securing the company's data and user identities
Compute can automatically scale down during low-demand periods
questions.explanation: Under the shared responsibility model the customer always keeps responsibility for their own data, identities, and access, in every service model — so this line in the business case is simply wrong. The other three are genuine, well-documented benefits: agility (provisioning in minutes), high availability (zone-redundant deployment), and elasticity (automatic scale-down). Each of those is phrased with a hedge ('can'), which is exactly how a realistic benefit statement should read.
questions.whyTested: Rather than asking you to recite benefits, this puts one false claim among three true ones written in the same confident business-case voice. The trap is that 'Microsoft takes over security' sounds like a selling point until you remember the shared responsibility model never hands the customer's data and identities to the provider — an idea AZ-900 tests from several angles.

questions.question: A company wants to avoid vendor lock-in as much as possible while still gaining cloud cost savings. Which general guidance is most accurate?
options: Signing a Reserved Instance commitment is what creates vendor lock-in, not the service model chosen
IaaS workloads are generally easier to move between providers than deeply-integrated PaaS/SaaS workloads, though some lock-in risk always exists
Lock-in risk is the same across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, since all three run on Microsoft-owned datacenters
Choosing PaaS over IaaS whenever possible minimizes lock-in, since PaaS abstracts away the underlying infrastructure
questions.explanation: IaaS resources are closer to raw infrastructure and generally port more easily than workloads built around a provider's specific PaaS or SaaS features. PaaS abstracting the infrastructure is exactly what deepens lock-in, not what reduces it, and lock-in risk very much differs by service model — a Reserved Instance is a pricing choice with no bearing on portability.
questions.whyTested: This question buries the actual concept, that IaaS ports more easily than PaaS, inside distractors that sound authoritative, like 'lock-in is the same across all models' or 'Reserved Instances create lock-in,' to test whether you can isolate the real driver of portability from plausible-sounding noise that name-drops adjacent AZ-900 concepts like pricing commitments.

questions.question: A company has Dev, Test, and Prod subscriptions and wants one policy requiring 'US regions only' applied consistently across all three, without configuring it three separate times or affecting other subscriptions outside this company's tenant. Where should it be assigned?
options: At the tenant root management group, since policy can only be scoped to an entire tenant
At each resource group individually, since policy cannot be assigned above the resource group level
Only through RBAC role assignments on each subscription
At a management group containing exactly these three subscriptions
questions.explanation: Management groups let you assign governance once and have it flow down to every subscription beneath them — creating one scoped to just these three subscriptions avoids configuring it three times AND avoids affecting anything outside that group. The tenant root group would work but is broader than needed; policy can absolutely be scoped above the resource group level; and RBAC controls permissions, not configuration rules like allowed regions.

questions.question: A team needs compute for a task that runs unpredictably, roughly twice a month, triggered by an uploaded file, and finishes in under 10 minutes each time. Which is the most cost-effective choice?
options: A single reserved-capacity VM instance
A VM Scale Set with a fixed minimum of 5 instances
Azure Functions (serverless)
A permanently running virtual machine
questions.explanation: Serverless Functions only bill for actual execution time, making them far more cost-effective than infrastructure that runs constantly for a task that fires a couple of times a month. A Scale Set with a fixed minimum still keeps 5 instances running at all times, and reserving capacity commits to paying for a VM whether or not the trigger ever fires.

questions.question: A company needs its on-premises network connected to Azure with predictable, low latency, avoiding the public internet entirely, for a latency-sensitive workload. Which service fits best?
options: VPN Gateway
A Virtual WAN hub connecting sites over the internet
Azure Front Door
ExpressRoute
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection that doesn't traverse the public internet, giving the most predictable latency of the options here. VPN Gateway and an internet-based Virtual WAN hub both route over the public internet, and Front Door is a global entry point for web applications, not a site-to-site connectivity service.

questions.question: Two VMs host a stateful application whose instance count must stay at exactly two. The team wants protection from a single host or rack failure, and wants to avoid both VMs rebooting during the same planned maintenance, all within one datacenter. Which option fits?
options: Place both VMs in an availability set
Create a Virtual Machine Scale Set with autoscale rules
Put both VMs behind an Azure Load Balancer
Deploy the two VMs in two different regions
questions.explanation: An availability set spreads a fixed group of VMs across fault domains (separate racks, power, and switches) and update domains (separate maintenance windows) inside one datacenter — precisely the two protections asked for, with no change to instance count. A Scale Set is built to add and remove identical instances on demand, which conflicts with a fixed count of two stateful servers. A Load Balancer distributes traffic but has no say over where the VMs are physically placed. Two regions would protect against far more than a rack failure but adds latency and complexity the scenario never asked for.

questions.question: A company keeps seven years of compliance archives that are almost never opened. If an auditor requests one, retrieval within a day is acceptable. Storage cost must be as low as possible. Which blob access tier fits?
options: Hot
Cool
Cold
Archive
questions.explanation: Archive has the lowest storage cost of all tiers, and its trade-off — data is offline and must be rehydrated, which can take hours — is acceptable when a day's retrieval window is fine. Cold is the nearest miss: it is also for rarely accessed data, but it stays online with millisecond access and costs more to store than Archive, so it isn't the lowest-cost choice here. Cool is for data accessed occasionally, and Hot is priced for frequent access — both would pay for responsiveness the scenario explicitly doesn't need.

questions.question: A company's backups must survive the loss of an entire Azure region. The budget owner asks whether zone-redundant storage (ZRS) alone meets that requirement, since it already keeps three copies. Which response is accurate?
options: No — ZRS keeps every copy inside one region; GRS or GZRS adds a copy in the paired region
Yes — the three ZRS copies are placed in zones that Azure spreads across separate regions
Yes — ZRS fails over automatically to the paired region during a regional outage
No — only LRS can be combined with a paired region for cross-region replication
questions.explanation: ZRS protects against a datacenter (zone) failure by spreading copies across availability zones, but all of those zones belong to the same region, so a regional outage takes every copy with it. Surviving that needs geo-redundancy — GRS or GZRS — which adds asynchronous replication to the paired region. Zones never span regions, ZRS has no cross-region failover to perform, and LRS is the least redundant option, not a prerequisite for geo-replication.
questions.whyTested: The exam likes to test whether 'three copies' sounds like enough to you. ZRS and GRS both keep multiple copies; the discriminating fact is how far apart those copies are, and the wrong options each offer a plausible-sounding mechanism (zones in separate regions, automatic failover) that would let ZRS do a job it cannot.

questions.question: A company wants every engineer to get their own isolated Azure environment for testing, with the company's security policies applied automatically without extra configuration per environment. Which combination enables this?
options: Separate subscriptions per engineer, grouped under a management group with policy assigned at that level
Separate resource groups per engineer within one subscription, with the same policy assigned individually to each resource group
One resource group shared by all engineers with individual RBAC roles
A separate management group per engineer, each containing its own single subscription with no shared parent
questions.explanation: Subscriptions give real isolation, and a management group above them lets policy apply automatically to every subscription beneath it — configured once, not per environment. Assigning policy to each resource group individually technically works but requires exactly the repeated configuration the scenario wants to avoid, and separate management groups with no shared parent would still mean setting the policy up once per engineer.

questions.question: Which identity feature lets a partner organization's employees sign into your app using their own company credentials, without you creating accounts for them in your directory?
options: Conditional Access
External identities
Azure RBAC
A dynamic security group
questions.explanation: External identities let outside users authenticate with their own existing identity rather than a new account in your directory. Conditional Access and RBAC both assume the user already has some identity in your system; a dynamic security group just auto-manages membership for accounts that already exist.

questions.question: A company wants to require MFA only when an employee signs in from a country they've never signed in from before, but not on every sign-in. Which feature enables this specific, condition-based rule?
options: Conditional Access
External identities
Enabling multifactor authentication for all users
Azure RBAC
questions.explanation: Conditional Access applies rules based on conditions like sign-in location, layering MFA on only when a condition is met. Enabling MFA for all users would require it on every sign-in regardless of location, which is more than this scenario asks for.

questions.question: A contractor signs in to the Azure portal from a compliant laptop but gets 'access denied' when restarting a VM. From an unmanaged tablet, the sign-in itself is blocked before the portal loads. Which pairing explains the two outcomes?
options: The restart failure is an Azure RBAC gap; the blocked tablet sign-in is Conditional Access
The restart failure is Conditional Access; the blocked tablet sign-in is an Azure RBAC gap
Both outcomes come from Conditional Access evaluating the device and the action
Both outcomes come from Azure RBAC, since role assignments can be scoped to a device
questions.explanation: The contractor could sign in from the laptop, so Conditional Access let them through; being unable to restart a VM once inside is a missing permission, which is RBAC's domain. Blocking the sign-in entirely from an unmanaged device is a device-compliance condition — classic Conditional Access, evaluated before any resource is touched. Conditional Access decides whether and how a sign-in happens; it does not grant or deny individual resource actions. RBAC assigns roles to identities at a scope such as a resource group, never to a device.
questions.whyTested: Rather than asking for definitions, this gives two symptoms and asks you to attribute each to the right control. The hinge is sequence: Conditional Access acts at sign-in, RBAC acts on resource operations afterward — the exam checks that you can place each tool at its stage rather than just knowing both names.

questions.question: A scenario describes an attacker compromising the network perimeter, but still being unable to access application data without passing separate identity and device checks. Which principle does this describe?
options: A perimeter-based security model
Zero Trust
Least-privilege access
Network segmentation with NSGs
questions.explanation: Zero Trust means never assuming trust based on network location — every request is verified on identity, device, and context, so breaching the perimeter alone grants nothing. A perimeter-based model is the opposite assumption: once inside, traffic is trusted, which is exactly what fails here. Least privilege limits how much an already-authenticated identity can do, but it isn't the principle that demands separate identity and device checks on each request. NSG segmentation filters network traffic by IP and port; it does not verify who or what device is making the request.

questions.question: A new administrator is asked to produce, with no setup work, a list of concrete changes to existing resources that would cut cost, improve resilience, and tighten security, based on Azure's own analysis of their configuration. Which tool should they open first?
options: Azure Monitor
Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Azure Advisor
An Azure Well-Architected Review assessment
questions.explanation: Advisor continuously analyzes your deployed resources and surfaces specific recommendations across cost, reliability, performance, security, and operational excellence — free and with nothing to configure. Defender for Cloud is the near-miss: it also recommends changes, but only for security posture, so it misses the cost and resilience asks. Monitor collects metrics and logs and raises alerts; it doesn't recommend configuration changes. A Well-Architected Review is a questionnaire-based self-assessment of a workload's design, not an automated scan of what is actually deployed.

questions.question: A company needs to move 200 TB of on-premises data into Azure Blob Storage, but their internet connection would take months to transfer it. Which service is designed for this scenario?
options: Azure File Sync
Azure Migrate
Azure Data Box
AzCopy over a site-to-site VPN
questions.explanation: Data Box is a physical device for transferring very large datasets offline when network transfer isn't practical. AzCopy over a VPN is still limited by the same slow internet connection — it doesn't solve the bottleneck, just moves it onto an encrypted tunnel.

questions.question: Which tool would an administrator use to script bulk, one-time file copies between an on-premises server and Azure Blob Storage from the command line?
options: Azure File Sync
AzCopy
Azure Migrate
Azure Storage Explorer
questions.explanation: AzCopy is the command-line tool built for scripted transfers. Storage Explorer offers similar transfer capability but through a GUI, not a script; File Sync is for ongoing, continuous synchronization rather than a one-time scripted copy; and Migrate is for assessing and moving whole workloads, not files.

questions.question: A company wants to manage on-premises servers and VMs in another cloud using the same Azure tools, like Azure Policy and RBAC, that they already use for native Azure resources. Which service enables this?
options: Azure Monitor
Azure Migrate
A hybrid Microsoft Entra Connect deployment
Azure Arc
questions.explanation: Azure Arc extends Azure management tooling — including Policy and RBAC — to resources outside Azure. Migrate assesses and moves workloads rather than managing them afterward, Monitor only collects telemetry, and Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizes identities, not resource governance.

questions.question: A company deploys VMs across two availability zones in the same region for resilience. Which failure scenario would this NOT protect against?
options: A single rack failing within one zone
A single datacenter losing power
A cooling failure in one zone's datacenter
The entire Azure region becoming unavailable
questions.explanation: Availability zones protect against datacenter-level failures within a region — power, cooling, or a single rack going down in one zone — because the other zone keeps running. They don't protect against a failure of the region itself, which needs geo-redundancy or a multi-region design.

questions.question: An application needs to authenticate a service, not a person, to access Azure resources without embedding a password in code. Which Entra ID feature fits?
options: A guest user account created for the application
Self-service password reset applied to a service account
A dynamic security group containing the application
A managed identity
questions.explanation: A managed identity lets an Azure resource authenticate to other services automatically, with Azure handling the credential entirely — nothing is embedded in code. The other three all still rely on a password or an account meant for a human, which is exactly what this scenario is trying to avoid.

questions.question: A company wants to prevent a storage account holding compliance data from ever being deleted, even by an administrator who has full Owner permissions on the subscription. Which feature should they apply?
options: A Delete resource lock
An Azure Policy with an Audit effect
Removing the Owner role from all administrators
A Read-only lock, since it is a stricter version of Delete
questions.explanation: A resource lock overrides normal RBAC permissions to prevent deletion, regardless of what a user's role otherwise allows — a Delete lock is exactly targeted at this requirement. Removing Owner roles is impractical and self-defeating; an Audit-effect policy only reports non-compliance without blocking anything; and a Read-only lock is stricter in a different way (it also blocks modification) but isn't 'more Delete' than a Delete lock.

questions.question: A company wants to both enforce a rule, like 'no VMs outside East US,' and separately get recommendations for improving cost efficiency of existing resources. Which combination is correct?
options: Azure Policy for both, since it can also generate cost recommendations
Azure Monitor for enforcement, Azure Policy for recommendations
Azure Advisor for both, since it can also enforce configuration rules
Azure Policy for enforcement, Azure Advisor for recommendations
questions.explanation: Policy enforces configuration rules going forward; Advisor analyzes existing resources and recommends improvements. Policy doesn't generate recommendations, and Advisor doesn't block or enforce anything — each tool does only one half of this scenario.

questions.question: A company needs to discover and classify sensitive data, like customer SSNs, scattered across multiple data stores in a hybrid environment. Which service is purpose-built for this?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Azure Policy, using a policy that audits storage account configurations
Azure Advisor, under its security recommendations
Microsoft Purview
questions.explanation: Purview is specifically for discovering, classifying, and protecting sensitive data, including across hybrid sources. Policy and Advisor both operate on resource configuration, not the content stored inside resources, and Defender for Cloud focuses on threat protection and security posture rather than data classification.

questions.question: An administrator wants to run Azure management commands from a browser on a locked-down machine where they cannot install software. Which tool fits?
options: The Azure mobile app
Azure Cloud Shell
Azure PowerShell
Azure CLI
questions.explanation: Cloud Shell runs entirely in the browser with nothing to install, unlike CLI or PowerShell, which are installed locally (though both are also available for use from within Cloud Shell). The Azure mobile app supports monitoring and basic actions, but not the same scripting/command experience.

questions.question: A team deploys environments with a long Azure CLI script that creates resources one by one. Re-running it after a partial failure errors out because some resources already exist. They want deployments that can be safely re-run and whose intended end state lives in source control. What should they adopt?
options: Declarative templates such as ARM or Bicep
A Read-only lock applied after each successful run
A longer CLI script with delete steps before each create
Azure Advisor operational-excellence recommendations
questions.explanation: ARM and Bicep templates are declarative: they describe the desired end state, and Resource Manager works out what to create, update, or leave alone, so re-running the same template is safe (idempotent) and the file itself is the version-controlled source of truth. The imperative CLI script is the near-miss — it can also be stored in source control, but it describes steps, not a state, which is why a re-run collides with what already exists. Adding delete-then-create steps makes re-runs destructive rather than safe. A Read-only lock protects what was deployed but doesn't make deployment repeatable, and Advisor can suggest improvements but never deploys anything.

questions.question: Which Azure tool would specifically flag that a company is paying for several unattached, unused disks?
options: Microsoft Purview
Azure Service Health
Azure Policy, if configured to deny disk creation
Azure Advisor
questions.explanation: Azure Advisor analyzes usage and cost, and will flag unused resources like orphaned disks as a cost-saving opportunity. A deny-effect Policy could stop new unattached disks from being created going forward, but it doesn't flag ones that already exist, and neither Purview nor Service Health looks at resource utilization at all.

questions.question: A company wants to know immediately if there's an ongoing Azure platform outage affecting a region they use, separate from the health of their own individual resources. Which service fits?
options: Microsoft Purview
Azure Service Health
Azure Monitor, using its resource health alerts
Azure Advisor
questions.explanation: Service Health reports on the health of the Azure platform itself. Azure Monitor's resource health signal is about your own resource's connectivity to the platform, not whether Azure's infrastructure in that region is having a broader outage — a subtle but real distinction.

questions.question: A web app in West Europe starts returning errors minutes after a deployment. Before rolling back, the on-call engineer wants to rule out a problem on Microsoft's side. Which tool answers whether the cause is a platform incident rather than their own release?
options: Azure Service Health
Azure Monitor metrics for the App Service
Azure Advisor reliability recommendations
Microsoft Defender for Cloud's secure score
questions.explanation: Service Health reports incidents, planned maintenance, and advisories affecting the Azure platform itself, filtered to the regions and services you use — the one place that says 'Microsoft has an active issue in West Europe.' Monitor metrics are the near-miss: they would confirm the error rate climbed, but they describe your resource's symptoms, not whether the platform underneath is at fault. Advisor offers longer-term design recommendations, not live incident status, and secure score measures security posture, which has nothing to do with an outage.

questions.question: A finance team wants monthly spending broken down by department, using labels applied to each resource when it was created. Which feature enables this, combined with Cost Management?
options: Management groups, since cost naturally rolls up by group
A separate subscription per department
Resource locks
Tags
questions.explanation: Tags are name/value pairs applied directly to a resource and used to filter cost reports by whatever label you choose, like department. A separate subscription per department would also let you break down cost, but it's a much heavier restructuring than 'labels applied to each resource' calls for, and management groups organize subscriptions for governance, not cost tagging.

questions.question: Which of these would Azure Policy be best suited to enforce?
options: Automatically scale a VM Scale Set based on CPU usage
Notify the security team when a login occurs from a new country
Every new storage account must use only approved SKUs
Give a specific user permission to restart VMs but nothing else
questions.explanation: The other three describe RBAC (a scoped permission grant), Conditional Access or an alert rule (a sign-in condition triggering a notification), and autoscaling respectively. Only the first is a standing configuration rule evaluated against resources — exactly what Azure Policy enforces.

questions.question: A production resource group carries a Delete lock. An administrator who is an Owner on the subscription must urgently delete one VM inside that group. Which sequence is correct?
options: Remove the lock, delete the VM, then re-apply the lock
Delete the VM directly, since Owner rights override the lock
Switch the lock to Read-only, which allows deletion but not edits
Wait for the lock to expire, since locks are time-limited
questions.explanation: Locks apply regardless of RBAC role — even an Owner cannot delete through one — and a lock on a resource group is inherited by every resource inside it, so the VM is covered. The only path is to remove (or temporarily remove) the lock, perform the deletion, and put it back; Owner or User Access Administrator rights are what allow managing the lock itself. A Read-only lock is stricter, not looser: it blocks modification and deletion. Locks never expire on their own.

questions.question: An architect wants one place to see health, performance, and log data across VMs, App Services, and databases, with the ability to configure alerts. Which service fits?
options: Azure Advisor
Azure Monitor
Azure Service Health
Microsoft Purview
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor is the unified telemetry, logging, and alerting service across your own resources. Service Health reports on the Azure platform rather than your workloads, Advisor gives point-in-time recommendations rather than ongoing telemetry, and Purview is focused on data governance, not resource health.

questions.question: Which Azure Monitor component would you use to write a custom query against collected log data to find failed login attempts in the last 24 hours?
options: Application Insights
Log Analytics
Azure Advisor
Azure Service Health
questions.explanation: Log Analytics is the querying and storage layer within Azure Monitor for exactly this kind of custom log query. Application Insights is scoped to application performance telemetry specifically, and Advisor/Service Health don't support custom log querying at all.

questions.question: A company is deploying identical infrastructure to Dev, Test, and Prod and wants a guarantee that all three are configured identically, with the deployment definition stored in source control. Which approach fits best?
options: An Azure Policy that audits each environment for drift after deployment
Infrastructure as Code using ARM templates
Azure Advisor recommendations
A single shared resource lock across all three
questions.explanation: IaC stored in source control is what guarantees identical, repeatable, trackable deployments across environments in the first place. An auditing policy could catch drift after the fact, but only once it's already happened — it doesn't guarantee the initial deployments matched, which is what this scenario asks for.

questions.question: An Azure Policy blocks creation of any VM without a 'CostCenter' tag, and a developer's deployment fails as a result. What does this indicate about the policy's effect setting?
options: It's using an Append effect, which adds the missing tag automatically
Policy cannot block deployments, only report on them
It's using an Audit-only effect, which only reports non-compliance
It's using a Deny effect
questions.explanation: A Deny effect actively blocks non-compliant deployments — the deployment failing is the tell. Audit only reports non-compliance without stopping it, and Append would add the missing tag automatically rather than blocking the deployment outright, so neither matches what happened here.

questions.question: A manager asks two questions: 'Exactly how much did the analytics team spend last month, by resource?' and 'Which of their VMs are oversized for their actual load?' Which tool answers each?
options: Cost Management cost analysis for the spend; Azure Advisor for the oversized VMs
Azure Advisor for the spend; Cost Management cost analysis for the oversized VMs
The Pricing calculator for the spend; Cost Management cost analysis for the oversized VMs
Cost Management cost analysis for both, since it includes right-sizing recommendations
questions.explanation: Cost analysis in Cost Management is the reporting tool for actual, historical spend, sliced by resource, tag, or time. Advisor is the tool that looks at utilization and recommends specific actions such as downsizing an underused VM. Swapping them fails because Advisor doesn't itemize invoices and cost analysis doesn't judge whether a VM is oversized. The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of resources you plan to deploy, not what you were actually billed, and cost analysis has no right-sizing logic of its own.

questions.question: In a PaaS deployment such as Azure SQL Database, responsibility for classifying the data and deciding who may access it transfers to Microsoft.
questions.explanation: Moving to PaaS hands Microsoft the operating system, database engine patching, and the underlying infrastructure — but data classification, identities, and access decisions stay with the customer in every service model, including SaaS. The misconception this statement encodes is that 'more managed' eventually means 'Microsoft owns the data responsibility'; the shared responsibility model never reaches that point.

questions.question: A virtual machine that has been stopped (deallocated) from the Azure portal continues to accrue compute charges until it is deleted.
questions.explanation: Under the consumption-based model, a deallocated VM releases its compute capacity and stops incurring compute charges; only its disks and any reserved public IP keep billing. The trap is the difference between stopping from the portal (deallocated, not billed for compute) and shutting down from inside the guest OS (still allocated, still billed) — the exam expects you to know that 'stopped' alone does not guarantee savings.

questions.question: In a PaaS service such as Azure App Service, the customer chooses when security patches are applied to the underlying guest operating system.
questions.explanation: Giving up control of the OS is the defining trade of PaaS: Microsoft patches the operating system and runtime on its own schedule, and in exchange the customer manages only the application and its data. A team that needs to control patch timing — for example to satisfy an audit window — needs IaaS, where the guest OS is theirs to patch. The statement describes IaaS-level control and misattributes it to PaaS.

questions.question: An Azure Functions app on the Consumption plan incurs compute charges continuously while it is deployed, even during hours in which no executions occur.
questions.explanation: Serverless billing is tied to execution: on the Consumption plan you pay per execution and for the compute consumed while code runs, and a function that is deployed but idle costs nothing in compute (its storage account still bills a small amount). This is what distinguishes serverless from a VM or an always-on App Service plan, which bill for provisioned capacity whether or not it is used. The statement applies the provisioned-capacity model to serverless, which is exactly the misconception the exam checks.

questions.question: Manually resizing a virtual machine from a D2 to a D4 size the night before a planned product launch is an example of elasticity.
questions.explanation: This is vertical scaling performed by hand — a legitimate example of scalability, since capacity was added to handle more load. Elasticity specifically means capacity expands and contracts automatically in response to real-time demand, with no administrator scheduling the change. A planned, manual resize fails the 'automatic' test, so calling it elasticity is the error the exam is probing for.

questions.question: Lifting-and-shifting on-premises servers to equivalently sized Azure VMs that run 24 hours a day captures the cloud's cost advantage on its own, because the billing is consumption-based.
questions.explanation: Consumption-based billing only saves money when consumption actually drops — by deallocating idle VMs, right-sizing, autoscaling, or moving to PaaS or serverless where appropriate. A like-for-like migration of always-on, fixed-size VMs reproduces the on-premises usage pattern in the cloud and can easily cost more than the hardware it replaced. The misconception here is treating pay-as-you-go as a discount in itself rather than an opportunity that still has to be exploited.

questions.question: Setting a Spot virtual machine's maximum price equal to the regular pay-as-you-go rate guarantees that Azure will never evict it.
questions.explanation: A Spot VM can be evicted for two reasons: the Spot price rising above your maximum, or Azure needing the capacity back. Setting the maximum price to the pay-as-you-go rate removes the first reason but not the second — a capacity-driven eviction can still happen with little notice at any price. That is why Spot is only suitable for interruption-tolerant work regardless of how the price cap is set, which is the point this statement gets wrong.

questions.question: If the region chosen for a resource group suffers an outage, the resources in that group that were deployed to other regions stop running as well.
questions.explanation: A resource group's region only determines where the group's metadata is stored. The resources inside can live in any region, and they keep running on their own regional infrastructure regardless of what happens to the metadata region — at most, management operations on the group could be affected while it is unreachable. The statement treats the group as a runtime boundary when it is only a logical management container.

questions.question: Deleting a resource group removes every resource it contains, and deleting a management group likewise removes the subscriptions beneath it.
questions.explanation: The first half is true and the second half is the trap. A resource group owns the lifecycle of its resources, so deleting it deletes everything inside. A management group is only an organizational container for subscriptions: it must be empty before it can be deleted, and moving subscriptions out of it (back to the tenant root group or elsewhere) leaves them intact. The exam likes to test that the two containers behave differently on deletion.

questions.question: Placing two virtual machines in the same availability set guarantees that they run in different availability zones.
questions.explanation: An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains and update domains — separate racks and separate maintenance windows — within a single datacenter. It says nothing about zones; both VMs can be, and normally are, in the same zone. Protection from a whole datacenter failing requires explicitly deploying the VMs into different availability zones, which is a separate choice (and the two options are mutually exclusive for a given VM). Confusing the two is one of the most common AZ-900 errors.

questions.question: A company that must encrypt its ExpressRoute traffic in transit has to configure that encryption itself — for example with IPsec or MACsec — because the circuit does not encrypt traffic by default.
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute's security comes from being a private, dedicated path that never touches the public internet, not from encryption. If a compliance rule requires encryption in transit, the customer adds it — a site-to-site VPN over the ExpressRoute private peering, or MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct. The contrast is VPN Gateway, which is encrypted (IPsec) precisely because it crosses the internet. Assuming 'private' means 'encrypted' is the mistake this statement is written to catch.

questions.question: An application using a storage account configured with geo-redundant storage (GRS) can read from the secondary region at any time, even before a failover is initiated.
questions.explanation: Plain GRS replicates data to the paired region, but that secondary copy is not accessible until a failover makes it the new primary. Read access to the secondary at any time is exactly what the read-access variants — RA-GRS and RA-GZRS — add, and that distinction is what you are paying for when you choose them. An app designed to serve reads from the secondary during a primary outage needs RA-GRS; with GRS it would simply fail until failover.

questions.question: Assigning an Azure Policy with a Deny effect automatically deletes existing resources that already violate the rule.
questions.explanation: Deny blocks new or updated deployments that would violate the rule. Resources that already exist are evaluated and reported as non-compliant on the policy's compliance dashboard, but Policy never deletes them. Bringing them into line is a separate remediation step — manual changes, or a remediation task for policies with DeployIfNotExists or Modify effects. The statement credits Policy with a destructive power it does not have, which is a frequent misconception.

questions.question: Adding a private endpoint to an Azure SQL Database automatically disables the database's public endpoint.
questions.explanation: A private endpoint adds a private IP for the service inside your VNet, so traffic from that network stays on the Microsoft backbone — but it is an addition, not a replacement. The public endpoint remains reachable until you separately turn off public network access (or restrict it with firewall rules). Teams that stop after creating the private endpoint have not actually reduced internet exposure, which is the gap this statement tests.

questions.question: A Conditional Access policy can require multifactor authentication from a user who holds no Azure RBAC role in any subscription.
questions.explanation: Conditional Access operates in Microsoft Entra ID at sign-in time and can be scoped to any user, group, or application — it has no dependency on Azure RBAC, which only governs what an identity can do with Azure resources after signing in. A user with zero Azure role assignments can still be required to pass MFA to reach Microsoft 365 or any other cloud app. Treating the two as linked, or assuming Conditional Access only matters for Azure administrators, is the misconception here.

questions.question: A subscription-level policy that denies resources outside East US can be overridden by assigning a more permissive allowed-locations policy at a resource group beneath it.
questions.explanation: Policy assignments accumulate down the hierarchy; they do not replace one another. A resource in that resource group is evaluated against both assignments, and the subscription-level Deny still blocks anything outside East US no matter what the lower-scope policy allows. A lower scope can only add restrictions, never loosen inherited ones — relaxing the rule for one group requires changing or exempting the higher assignment itself. The statement assumes 'closest scope wins,' which is how some systems work but not Azure Policy.

questions.question: A Delete lock applied to a resource group blocks deletion of the group itself but still allows individual resources inside it to be deleted.
questions.explanation: Locks are inherited by everything beneath the scope they are applied to, so a Delete lock on a resource group protects the group and every resource in it — the most restrictive lock in the chain applies. That inheritance is what makes a group-level lock useful for protecting a whole production workload with one setting. The statement imagines the lock as attached only to the container object, which would leave its contents unprotected; a Delete lock does still allow modification, but not deletion at any level.

questions.question: Azure Advisor can flag a single-instance virtual machine as a reliability risk, but it will not move that VM into an availability set or availability zone for you.
questions.explanation: Advisor is a recommendation engine: it analyzes configuration and usage and tells you what to change — a lone VM with no redundancy is a classic reliability finding — but it never alters resources. Acting on a finding is a separate step you take (or automate) yourself, which is also why Advisor recommendations tend to pile up unactioned in real subscriptions. The misconception on the other side would be expecting Advisor to remediate like a Policy remediation task or an Automation runbook; it does neither.

questions.question: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is the service you would use to scan an on-premises SQL Server and classify which columns contain credit-card numbers across a hybrid data estate.
questions.explanation: Discovering, scanning, and classifying sensitive data across hybrid and multi-cloud sources is Microsoft Purview's job — it builds a data map and applies classifications such as credit-card or national-ID patterns. Defender for Cloud is a security-posture and threat-protection tool: it can tell you a SQL server is misconfigured or under attack (and can reach on-premises servers through Azure Arc), but it is not the data-governance catalog that labels what each column contains. Both services touch 'security' and 'hybrid,' which is why the exam pairs them as distractors.

questions.question: Redeploying an unchanged ARM template to a resource group that already matches it creates a second copy of each resource.
questions.explanation: ARM templates are declarative and idempotent: Resource Manager compares the template's desired state with what exists and makes only the changes needed, so redeploying an unchanged template results in no changes rather than duplicates. That property is the whole reason templates are safer to re-run than an imperative script of create commands, which would collide with existing resources. The statement describes how a naive script behaves and misapplies it to IaC.

questions.question: Applying a CostCenter tag to a resource changes which subscription that resource's charges are billed to.
questions.explanation: Tags are metadata used to organize, filter, and report — in Cost Management you can group or filter spend by a tag such as CostCenter, which is exactly how chargeback reports are built. They never affect how a resource runs or where it is billed: charges always accrue to the subscription the resource lives in. Moving charges to a different subscription requires moving the resource itself. The statement confuses labeling spend for reporting with actually redirecting the invoice.

questions.question: A team is listing which parts of its proposed Azure design will never require them to patch an operating system. Which two services in the design meet that bar? (Choose two.)
options: Azure SQL Database
SQL Server installed on an Azure virtual machine
Azure App Service
Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database and App Service are PaaS: Microsoft owns the operating system and runtime patching, and the team manages only data and code. SQL Server on a VM is the near-miss — it is the same database engine, but running on IaaS, so the guest OS (and the engine itself) are the customer's to patch. Azure Virtual Desktop is a managed service for the brokering and gateway layer, but its session hosts are VMs in the customer's subscription whose Windows OS the customer still patches.

questions.question: A CTO drafts five expected outcomes of moving a line-of-business app to Azure. Which two are realistic expectations? (Choose two.)
options: Extra capacity can be added within minutes rather than after a procurement cycle
Microsoft assumes responsibility for classifying and protecting the company's data
Deploying across availability zones can raise availability beyond a single datacenter
The monthly bill becomes fixed and predictable regardless of how much is used
The service SLA guarantees the app will experience zero downtime
questions.explanation: Agility (provisioning in minutes) and higher availability through zone-redundant deployment are genuine, documented benefits. The other three each encode a common misconception: data classification and protection stay with the customer under the shared responsibility model; consumption-based billing makes cost track usage, which is the opposite of fixed — predictability comes from managing it, not from the model itself; and an SLA is a commitment with service credits for missed targets, never a zero-downtime guarantee.
