Surviving a failure of the whole region requires a separate region entirely — an Availability Zone can't help once the region itself is down. Resource groups and scale sets are organizational/scaling constructs, not fault-isolation boundaries.

caseStudies.title: Fabrikam Manufacturing Evaluates Cloud Adoption
caseStudies.scenario: Fabrikam Manufacturing currently runs its order-management application on aging servers in a single on-premises datacenter that it owns and maintains outright. The finance team is frustrated that every hardware refresh means a large upfront purchase, and they'd rather spend based on actual monthly usage instead. Demand for the app is unpredictable — it's quiet most of the year but spikes hard during quarterly inventory counts — and the current servers are sized (and paid for) to handle the worst-case spike even though they sit mostly idle the rest of the time. Compliance also requires certain manufacturing records to remain on hardware Fabrikam controls directly, even as the company plans to move everything else it can to the cloud. Separately, Fabrikam wants a security model where, once the cloud migration happens, it never has to worry about patching the operating system of the servers running its web front end.

questions.question: Which shift best describes what the finance team wants, moving away from large upfront hardware purchases toward paying only for what's actually used each month?
options: Moving from capital expenditure (CapEx) to operational expenditure (OpEx)
Moving from operational expenditure (OpEx) to capital expenditure (CapEx)
Increasing total cost of ownership (TCO)
Adopting a private cloud deployment model
questions.explanation: CapEx is the large upfront spend on owned hardware; OpEx is the ongoing, consumption-based spending model the cloud enables — exactly the direction finance wants to move. The reverse direction, OpEx to CapEx, describes going back to owned hardware, and this scenario isn't about TCO increasing or about a private cloud deployment (which would still mean owning the infrastructure).

questions.question: True or false: because demand is quiet most of the year and only spikes during quarterly inventory counts, sizing and paying for fixed capacity that covers the worst-case spike year-round is the cost-effective approach here.
questions.explanation: This is precisely the problem elasticity solves: automatically scaling capacity up for the spike and back down afterward means Fabrikam pays close to actual usage instead of paying for peak capacity it barely uses most of the year. Provisioning fixed, worst-case capacity year-round is the expensive, on-premises pattern the scenario describes Fabrikam trying to escape, not a recommended cloud practice.

questions.question: Given that some manufacturing records must stay on hardware Fabrikam controls directly while the rest of its workloads move to the cloud, which cloud deployment model fits Fabrikam's overall plan?
options: Hybrid cloud
Public cloud only
Private cloud only
Multi-cloud
questions.explanation: Hybrid cloud is exactly the combination of retained on-premises/private infrastructure (for the records that must stay under Fabrikam's direct control) with public cloud for everything else. Public-cloud-only or private-cloud-only would each leave one of Fabrikam's two stated requirements unmet, and multi-cloud describes using multiple public cloud providers together, which isn't what's being described here.

questions.question: Fabrikam wants to never have to patch the operating system of the servers running its web front end after migrating. Which of the following statements about meeting this goal are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
options: Choosing a PaaS service, like Azure App Service, shifts OS patching responsibility to Microsoft
Choosing IaaS (VMs) would still leave Fabrikam responsible for guest-OS patching
The shared responsibility model means the customer always keeps some responsibility, even on PaaS, such as securing their own data and access
Any Azure compute option automatically removes all OS-patching responsibility from the customer
questions.explanation: PaaS services like Azure App Service manage the underlying OS and runtime, so Microsoft handles patching — a direct fit for Fabrikam's goal. IaaS VMs still put guest-OS patching on the customer, which is why PaaS (not IaaS) is the right choice here. The shared responsibility model never fully disappears — the customer always retains some responsibility, like their own data, identities, and access, regardless of service model. The last statement is false: responsibility shifts with service model, it doesn't vanish entirely on every option — IaaS in particular still leaves OS patching with the customer.
questions.whyTested: This question tests whether you can connect a stated business goal ("never patch the OS") to the specific service model that satisfies it, rather than just reciting the IaaS/PaaS/SaaS responsibility split in the abstract — and it also checks that you know the shared responsibility model never reaches zero customer responsibility, which the last, deliberately-too-absolute option is designed to catch.

compare.scenario: A retailer's web traffic triples every Black Friday weekend and returns to normal by Tuesday. They want to pay for the extra capacity only while it's actually needed. Which better describes the cloud benefit they are relying on?
compare.optionA: Scalability — the ability to add resources so the application can handle increased load.
compare.optionB: Elasticity — resources are added as demand rises and automatically removed again as it falls.
compare.why: Scalability is true but incomplete: it only says capacity can grow. The scenario stresses paying only while the surge lasts, which depends on capacity shrinking back afterward — that is Elasticity. On the exam, when a scenario mentions both the spike and the return to normal, elasticity is the sharper answer.

compare.scenario: A hospital must keep patient-record processing on servers it owns for regulatory reasons, but wants to run month-end analytics on Azure using copies of de-identified data. Which better describes the deployment model?
compare.optionA: Private cloud, because the sensitive workloads stay on hardware the hospital controls.
compare.optionB: Hybrid cloud, because on-premises systems and public cloud resources are used together for the same organization's workloads.
compare.why: The private-cloud answer describes only the most sensitive half of the picture. As soon as on-premises infrastructure and Azure are combined to serve one organization's workloads, the model as a whole is hybrid — the exam expects you to name the combined arrangement, not its most restricted part.

compare.scenario: A team needs to host a containerized API with no cluster to operate. It sits idle most of the day, with short bursts of traffic. Which is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), because it is Azure's managed container orchestrator.
compare.optionB: Azure Container Apps, because it runs containers without exposing an orchestrator and can scale to zero when idle.
compare.why: AKS is managed, but you still own node pools, upgrades, and cluster-level configuration — the scenario explicitly wants no cluster to operate. Container Apps hides the orchestrator entirely and scales to zero during idle hours, which also matches the burst-then-idle traffic pattern and its cost profile.

compare.scenario: An application stores millions of product images that are read far more often than written and must be served to users worldwide at the lowest practical cost. Which storage choice is better?
compare.optionA: Azure Files, because it provides a fully managed file share the application can mount.
compare.optionB: Azure Blob Storage, because it is object storage built for massive amounts of unstructured data.
compare.why: Azure Files would work, but it exists for SMB/NFS file-share semantics such as lift-and-shift apps and shared configuration, and is priced for that. Blob Storage is the service designed for unstructured objects like images at scale, with access tiers to cut cost on rarely-read files and native integration with a CDN for worldwide delivery.

compare.scenario: A company wants to guarantee that nobody — including subscription Owners — can create virtual machines outside the East US region. Which control is better?
compare.optionA: A custom RBAC role that grants VM permissions, assigned to every team that deploys infrastructure.
compare.optionB: An Azure Policy assignment with an allowed-locations rule at the subscription scope.
compare.why: RBAC answers who may perform which actions; it cannot express a condition like "only in this region," and an Owner can grant themselves more rights anyway. Azure Policy evaluates the properties of what is being deployed (such as location) and applies to everyone at that scope, Owners included — exactly what the scenario asks for.

compare.scenario: A finance team wants to be warned before monthly Azure spend passes $10,000, ideally based on a forecast early in the month rather than after the money is gone. Which tool is better?
compare.optionA: Azure Advisor cost recommendations, which identify underused resources that are inflating the bill.
compare.optionB: A Cost Management budget with alert thresholds, which notifies when actual or forecasted spend crosses a limit.
compare.why: Advisor's cost recommendations are useful but reactive — they suggest right-sizing after the fact and never track a spend ceiling. A budget in Cost Management is the feature built to define a dollar limit and alert on actual or forecasted spend against it, which is the early warning the team asked for.

compare.scenario: A startup's developers can now stand up a complete test environment in ten minutes, where the old procurement process took six weeks. Nothing about the environment grows or shrinks once it exists. Which cloud benefit does this best illustrate?
compare.optionA: Elasticity — the platform provides capacity on demand so the team no longer waits for hardware.
compare.optionB: Agility — resources can be provisioned and changed quickly, shortening the time from idea to running environment.
compare.why: Agility is specifically about how fast you can provision and iterate, which is the whole story here: weeks to minutes. Elasticity sounds close because both involve getting capacity when you want it, but elasticity means capacity automatically expanding and contracting with demand — and the scenario says the environment does neither once it exists.

compare.scenario: A payments company must keep its core application running if the whole East US region becomes unavailable, accepting a few minutes of recovery time. Which design concept are they actually asking for?
compare.optionA: Disaster recovery — replicate the workload to a second region and fail over when the primary region is lost.
compare.optionB: High availability — spread the workload across availability zones so a datacenter failure does not interrupt service.
compare.why: Losing an entire region is the disaster-recovery scenario: it needs a second region to fail over to, and the stated tolerance for a few minutes of recovery time is the RTO that distinguishes DR from always-on availability. Zone-redundant high availability is the tempting pick because it is the more common resilience design, but every zone sits inside East US, so it offers nothing once the region itself is gone.

compare.scenario: Two VMs run a stateless web tier in one region. The team wants the site to stay up if one Azure datacenter in that region loses power, with no extra regions involved. Which placement is better?
compare.optionA: Deploy the VMs into two different availability zones in that region.
compare.optionB: Deploy the VMs into an availability set so they are spread across fault and update domains.
compare.why: An availability set spreads VMs across racks inside a single datacenter, so it survives a rack or host failure but not the whole building losing power. Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within the region, each with independent power and cooling — the only option here that meets 'one datacenter loses power.' The availability set is the near-miss because it is the older, better-known VM resilience feature.

compare.scenario: A 20-person branch office needs its network connected to an Azure VNet within a week, for ordinary file-sync and intranet traffic. Latency variation is acceptable, and the budget is small. Which connection is better?
compare.optionA: ExpressRoute, because it bypasses the public internet and gives the most predictable performance.
compare.optionB: A site-to-site VPN Gateway, because it is encrypted, inexpensive, and can be set up over the existing internet link in hours.
compare.why: A site-to-site VPN gives this office a secure, encrypted tunnel over its existing connection at low cost and within the week they have. ExpressRoute is genuinely superior on latency and isolation, which is why it tempts, but it requires a carrier-provisioned circuit that takes weeks and costs far more — and nothing in the scenario needs that: modest traffic, tolerance for variability, and a tight budget all point the other way.

compare.scenario: A production storage account must never be deleted by accident, but the operations team still changes its network rules and access tiers every week. Which protection is better?
compare.optionA: A Delete (CanNotDelete) lock on the storage account.
compare.optionB: A Read-only lock on the storage account, since it is the stricter of the two lock types.
compare.why: A Delete lock blocks exactly the one thing the team fears — deletion — while leaving every configuration change available, which matches the weekly rule and tier changes. The Read-only lock is the near-miss because 'stricter' feels safer, but it also blocks every modification, so the operations team's routine changes would start failing and someone would end up removing the lock altogether.

compare.scenario: An architect has sketched a specific Azure design — three VMs of a known size, a SQL database tier, and 2 TB of blob storage — and needs a monthly cost estimate for the proposal before anything is deployed. Which tool is better?
compare.optionA: The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator, since the design is not deployed yet and the cost is a projection.
compare.optionB: The Azure Pricing calculator, which prices out the specific services and sizes selected for the design.
compare.why: The Pricing calculator exists to build up an estimate from named services, SKUs, regions, and quantities — exactly what a sketched architecture provides. The TCO calculator looks appealing because the design is still a projection, but it answers a different question: what an existing on-premises estate would cost in Azure over several years versus staying put. It takes server counts and datacenter costs as input, not a planned Azure bill of materials.
